title: Flatline at 9:48
hook: Why would a dish of heart cells stop beating while it was swimming in sugar and oxygen?
briefing: Cells make ATP in stages. Glycolysis splits glucose in the cytoplasm and nets 2 ATP, no oxygen needed. The Krebs cycle loads electrons onto NADH and FADH2. The electron transport chain passes those electrons to oxygen and powers ATP synthase, which makes most of the cell's ATP. If that last stage stops, cells fall back on fermentation. Keep all of that in mind. You'll need it in court.
intro: Hillcrest High, 7:02 a.m. Team Nova's heart-muscle cells, nicknamed the Drummers, beat in a dish for three weeks. This morning they're silent. The state science fair judges arrive at noon. Your lab partner Jules has pulled three witnesses into Room 204. Press their statements for details. When a line doesn't add up, present the evidence that breaks it. Five wrong calls and the case is closed without you.
outro_win: Margo's uncropped photo put her at the open dish with Buffer B at 9:45, three minutes before the flatline. She wanted a front-page sabotage scoop, and a rival to pin it on. Team Nova grows a backup dish and presents the case itself: oxygen everywhere, ATP in ruins, one poison at the end of the chain. The judges give it first place.
outro_lose: The wrong name makes the headline, and the real culprit gets the scoop. Go back to the numbers. Oxygen piled up unused, so the end of the chain was blocked. A poison like that works in minutes. Who was at the dish just minutes before 9:48?

content.premise: Team Nova grew real heart-muscle cells that beat in a dish. They were the favorite to win the state science fair. Last night, the cells stopped beating. They had sugar. They had oxygen. Three people were near Room 204. Cross-examine them before the judges arrive at noon.
content.setting: Room 204, the biology lab at Hillcrest High, the morning after the heart cells stopped

characters.name: Jules Tran
characters.bio: Your lab partner. Knows the class notes cold. Named the heart cells the Drummers and wants justice for them.

characters.name: Blake Okoro
characters.bio: Three-time science fair champ. Studies dead, preserved cells. His ego is very much alive.

characters.name: Gus Ferreira
characters.bio: Has cleaned Hillcrest for 22 years. Talks to his floor polisher, Duchess. Swears she listens.

characters.name: Margo Vance
characters.bio: Runs the school paper and the Heart Cam livestream of Team Nova's cells. Talks in headlines.

evidence.title: 7 A.M. Dish Check
evidence.detail: Cells still stuck to the dish, alive but barely. Not beating. Glucose: plenty left. Lactate: 8 times normal. ATP: 15% of normal.
evidence.key_fact: ATP at 15% of normal, lactate 8 times higher

evidence.title: Front Door Swipe Log
evidence.detail: Room 204 front door, last night. Blake Okoro: in 6:30, out 7:30. Blake Okoro: in 9:05, out 9:10. Gus Ferreira: in 10:00, out 10:40.

evidence.title: Incubator Temperature Log
evidence.detail: Steady at 37 °C all evening. Power off 10:05 to 10:25 p.m., dipping to 33 °C. Back to 37 °C by 10:30 and steady all night.
evidence.key_fact: Cooled to 33 °C for 20 minutes, then fully rewarmed

evidence.title: Oxygen Probe Readings
evidence.detail: Oxygen in Nova's dish, read hourly. A normal night stays near 110, because busy cells pull oxygen out. Last night: 9 p.m. 110. 10 p.m. 150. 7 a.m. 155.
evidence.key_fact: Oxygen in the dish went UP overnight

evidence.title: Rubber Doorstop
evidence.detail: Found wedging Room 204's back door open last night. The back door has no card reader.
evidence.key_fact: Back-door visitors never show up in the swipe log

evidence.title: Heart Monitor Printout
evidence.detail: Beats per minute from Nova's dish. Steady at 60 from 6:00 to 9:46 p.m. 9:47: 31. 9:48: 0. Alarm on. No beats since.

evidence.title: Bottle of Buffer B
evidence.detail: Found in the trash by Nova's incubator, cap off, half empty. Label: "Contains sodium azide. Blocks cells like cyanide. For dead, preserved cells ONLY."
evidence.key_fact: Sodium azide: blocks the same step as cyanide

evidence.title: Tribune Safety Story
evidence.detail: Last month's front page, by Margo Vance: "The Scariest Bottle in Room 204." Photo of Buffer B on Blake's shelf, label circled in red.
evidence.key_fact: Margo knew exactly where Buffer B was kept

evidence.title: Margo's Uncropped Photo
evidence.detail: Full version of Margo's "SABOTAGE" photo, shot up close. Nova's dish with the lid off, Buffer B uncapped beside it. Photo data: 9:45 p.m., Room 204.
evidence.key_fact: Margo shot the open dish, Buffer B beside it, at 9:45

testimonies.title: Your Cells Are Just Lazy

statements.text: I was here from 6:30 to 7:30, staining MY cells. Dead ones. They don't complain.
statements.press_reply: Preserved cells, already dead. I rinse them with Buffer B from my shelf. Totally safe for them. They're past caring.

statements.text: When I left, your cells were beating like a drum solo. Not that I was looking.
statements.press_reply: Sixty beats a minute. I counted. Out of scientific curiosity. Not jealousy. Definitely not jealousy.

statements.text: I came back at 9:05 for my phone charger. In and out in five minutes.
statements.press_reply: Weird thing, though. The back door was propped open with a doorstop. Not my doing. I use doors like a civilized person.

statements.text: This morning your cells look lazy, not dead. They switched to fermentation.
statements.press_reply: They probably ran low on oxygen. Cells ferment when they can't breathe. Check the oxygen probe in your dish, genius.

statements.text: Fermentation is a backup generator. Same energy, different fuel. Nothing to cry about.
statements.press_reply: Glycolysis keeps chugging, fermentation keeps it going. Energy is energy. Honestly, your cells are having a spa day.

contradiction.explanation: Fermentation only recycles NAD+ so glycolysis can keep making its 2 ATP per glucose. Aerobic respiration makes about 30. The high lactate proves the cells were fermenting, and their ATP still crashed to 15%.

testimonies.breakthrough: Okay, okay. 2 ATP instead of 30 is not a spa day. Something shut down their mitochondria and forced them to ferment. But it wasn't me!
hints: Blake says everything with a smirk. Only one of his lines breaks the rules of biology.
Aerobic respiration makes about 30 ATP per glucose. Fermentation just keeps glycolysis running, and glycolysis makes 2.
If fermenting cells really had the same energy, what would their ATP look like this morning? Check what it actually was.

testimonies.title: Duchess Needed an Outlet

statements.text: I swiped in at ten sharp, like always. Duchess and I keep a tight schedule.
statements.press_reply: Floors, then trash, then floors again. The back door was propped open, so I kicked the doorstop out. Drafts are bad for Duchess.

statements.text: At 10:05 I unplugged your incubator for twenty minutes. Duchess needs the good outlet.
statements.press_reply: Plugged it right back in at 10:25. A little chilly for twenty minutes, then toasty again. The temperature log will back me up.

statements.text: Your heart monitor was already beeping when I walked in. So I printed out its log.
statements.press_reply: Beeping like a microwave nobody's watching. I figured you kids would want the printout, so I saved it. You're welcome.

statements.text: Those cells suffocated, plain and simple. Not enough oxygen got into that dish.
statements.press_reply: My uncle's goldfish went the same way. No oxygen, no energy. That's biology, kid.

statements.text: Somebody tossed a bottle in the trash right next to your incubator. Didn't recognize it.
statements.press_reply: Cap off, half empty, scary label. I don't touch chemicals. Bagged it with gloves and saved it for you.

contradiction.explanation: Cells use oxygen at only one step: the end of the electron transport chain, where oxygen grabs electrons and becomes water. Oxygen in the dish went UP. It was right there. The cells just stopped using it.

testimonies.breakthrough: Wait. So there was plenty of oxygen, and the cells couldn't use it? Then the very end of the chain was jammed. That's no draft. That's poison!
hints: Gus has a simple answer. Ask yourself: was something missing, or was something just not being used?
Oxygen is used at one place only: the end of the electron transport chain, where it catches electrons and becomes water.
If cells stop using oxygen but it keeps flowing in, what happens to the amount in the dish? Is anything measuring that?

testimonies.title: BREAKING: I Know Who Did It

statements.text: I ran Heart Cam for my live blog last night. Your cells were the best story at Hillcrest.
statements.press_reply: Eleven live viewers! Well, ten and my mom. Turns out heartbeats are amazing content.

statements.text: Everybody knows Blake keeps Buffer B on his shelf. It's basically cyanide in a bottle.
statements.press_reply: I wrote a whole safety story about it last month. Photos, circled label, the works. Front page, obviously.

statements.text: Blake dosed your dish when he snuck back at 9:05. Poisons like that take a while to kick in.
statements.press_reply: Slow and sneaky, just like him. It crept up on your cells for ages, then boom. Flatline. Classic.

statements.text: At 9:52 I posted "SABOTAGE AT HILLCREST!" with an exclusive photo. Call it a reporter's instinct.
statements.press_reply: My best shot ever. I cropped it for drama, but the full version is even better. Here, look. I'm very proud.

statements.text: Blake had motive, means, and opportunity. Honestly, the headline writes itself.
statements.press_reply: Motive: he hates losing. Means: Buffer B. Opportunity: 9:05. I learned that from a true-crime podcast. Seven seasons.

contradiction.explanation: Sodium azide blocks complex IV, just like cyanide. The chain stops at once, ATP synthase stalls, and ATP crashes within minutes. The cells beat normally until 9:46. The dish was dosed around 9:45, not 9:05.

testimonies.breakthrough: Fine! If it hits in minutes, someone dosed the dish around 9:45, and Blake was long gone. But you can't prove who was there!
hints: Margo tells a great story. Check whether her timeline actually works.
A poison that blocks complex IV doesn't creep. The chain shuts down, and ATP collapses within minutes.
If the dish was poisoned when she says, when should the beating have stopped? Find the record of when it really did.

finale.question: Who poisoned Team Nova's heart cells?

options.label: No one. The cells ran out of sugar.

wrong_option_feedback.feedback: Buffer B is his, but he swiped out at 9:10. A complex IV poison crashes ATP within minutes, and the cells beat normally until 9:46. Someone opened that dish later.
Gus unplugged the incubator after the flatline. And mild cooling only slows enzymes. Warm them back up and they recover. These cells never did.
The 7 a.m. check shows plenty of glucose and 8 times the lactate. Glycolysis was running hard. The cells had fuel. They just couldn't use their oxygen.

finale.explanation: Sodium azide, like cyanide, blocks complex IV at the end of the electron transport chain. Electrons can't reach oxygen, so oxygen piles up unused. Proton pumping stops, ATP synthase stalls, and ATP crashes within minutes. The cells fell back on glycolysis and fermentation: only 2 ATP per glucose. Not enough to keep a heart beating.

field_guide.title: Glycolysis
field_guide.explanation: Splits one glucose into 2 pyruvate in the cytoplasm, netting 2 ATP and 2 NADH. Needs no oxygen.

field_guide.title: Fermentation
field_guide.explanation: When the chain can't run, cells turn pyruvate into lactate to recycle NAD+. Glycolysis keeps going, but that's only 2 ATP per glucose.

field_guide.title: Electron transport chain
field_guide.explanation: NADH and FADH2 hand electrons down proteins in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Oxygen catches them at the end and becomes water. No working chain, no oxygen use.

field_guide.title: Chemiosmosis and ATP synthase
field_guide.explanation: The chain pumps protons across the membrane. Protons flowing back through ATP synthase make most of the cell's ATP. Stop the chain and ATP synthase stalls.

field_guide.title: Electron transport chain poisons
field_guide.explanation: Cyanide and similar poisons block complex IV. Electrons can't reach oxygen, the whole chain stops, and ATP collapses within minutes.

field_guide.title: Enzymes and temperature
field_guide.explanation: Cooling slows enzymes, but they speed back up when warmed. High heat or extreme pH can denature them for good.
